final_answer.long_answer: Reference: [GG_1], [CRAWL_WIKI_1], [CRAWL_WIKI_2]. Detailed explanation: The provided context describes retinoschisis as an eye disease characterized by the splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers, usually in the outer plexiform layer. There are two main forms: a degenerative form which typically involves the peripheral retina and is not genetically inherited, and a hereditary form, known as X-linked juvenile or congenital retinoschisis. The hereditary form is due to an X-linked genetic defect in the RS1 gene, which encodes the retinoschisin protein that is vital for maintaining retinal cellular organization. Mutations in this gene lead to a malfunctioning protein and thus the development of the condition.

secondary to optic disc pit x linked juvenile retinoschisis secondary to optic disc pit this type of retinoschisis is very common with a prevalence of up to 7 percent in normal persons. its cause is unknown. it can easily be confused with retinal detachment by the non-expert observer and in difficult cases even the expert may have difficulty differentiating the two. such differentiation is important since retinal detachment almost always requires treatment while retinoschisis never itself requires treatment and leads to retinal detachment (and hence to visual loss) only occasionally. unfortunately one still sees cases of uncomplicated retinoschisis treated by laser retinopexy or cryopexy in an attempt to stop its progression towards the macula. such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. there is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. there is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. there is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. but as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. it is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an x-linked genetic defect. the genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called x-linked juvenile retinoschisis (xlrs) or congenital retinoschisis. affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] it is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. schisis is derived from the greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. however, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. if the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]
section: introduction
retinoschisis is an eye disease characterized by the abnormal splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers, usually in the outer plexiform layer. retinoschisis can be divided into degenerative forms which are very common and almost exclusively involve the peripheral retina and hereditary forms which are rare and involve the central retina and sometimes the peripheral retina. the degenerative forms are asymptomatic  and involve the peripheral retina only and do not affect the visual acuity. some rarer forms result in a loss of vision in the corresponding visual field.[1] almost all cases are x-linked recessive and caused by a mutation in the retinoschisin gene (rs1).[2]

section: introduction
retinoschisin also known as x-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the rs1 gene.[7] it is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] retinoschisin (rs1) is encoded by the gene rs1 located on the x chromosome at p22.1.[7] young males who have an rs1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an x-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
section: function
retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] in addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-atpase (na/k-atpase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] rs1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular map kinase signalling.[11]
section: clinical significance
pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for x-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] female carriers of the rs1 mutation do not show symptoms of x-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous x-chromosome inactivation. in young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] there are over 200 mutations of rs1 recorded in the retina international mutation database archived 2020-01-23 at the wayback machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

Section: Introduction
Retinoschisis is an eye disease characterized by the abnormal splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers, usually in the outer plexiform layer. Retinoschisis can be divided into degenerative forms which are very common and almost exclusively involve the peripheral retina and hereditary forms which are rare and involve the central retina and sometimes the peripheral retina. The degenerative forms are asymptomatic  and involve the peripheral retina only and do not affect the visual acuity. Some rarer forms result in a loss of vision in the corresponding visual field.[1] Almost all cases are X-linked recessive and caused by a mutation in the retinoschisin gene (RS1).[2]

Section: Classification

Familial foveal retinoschisis Exudative
Secondary to optic disc pit X linked juvenile retinoschisis Secondary to optic disc pit This type of retinoschisis is very common with a prevalence of up to 7 percent in normal persons. Its cause is unknown. It can easily be confused with retinal detachment by the non-expert observer and in difficult cases even the expert may have difficulty differentiating the two. Such differentiation is important since retinal detachment almost always requires treatment while retinoschisis never itself requires treatment and leads to retinal detachment (and hence to visual loss) only occasionally. Unfortunately one still sees cases of uncomplicated retinoschisis treated by laser retinopexy or cryopexy in an attempt to stop its progression towards the macula. Such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. There is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. There is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. Degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. There is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. But as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. It is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] Hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an X-linked genetic defect. The genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) or congenital retinoschisis. Affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] It is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. Schisis is derived from the Greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. However, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. If the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. Although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]

Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

llm.short_answer: Retinoschisis is an eye disorder characterized by splitting of the retina’s layers, and its genetic causes are primarily mutations in the RS1 gene.
llm.long_answer: Reference: [GG_2], [GG_3], [GG_4], [GG_16]. Detailed explanation: Retinoschisis is an eye condition defined by the abnormal splitting of the retinal neurosensory layers. In its hereditary form, particularly X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, the disease is caused by mutations in the RS1 gene. These mutations, which can include missense, nonsense, frameshift, and splice site mutations as well as deletions, disrupt the function of the RS1 protein that normally helps to hold the retinal layers together.

Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

llm.short_answer: retinoschisis is an eye disease characterized by splitting of the retinal layers; it is genetically caused by mutations in the RS1 gene on the X chromosome
llm.long_answer: Reference: [GG_8], [CRAWL_WIKI_2]. Detailed explanation: Retinoschisis is an eye disease marked by the abnormal splitting of the neurosensory layers of the retina. The genetic cause involves mutations in the RS1 gene, which is located on the X chromosome (specifically at Xp22.1). These mutations disrupt the production of retinoschisin, a protein crucial for maintaining retinal structure, leading to X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, primarily affecting young males.

Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

Section: Classification
Hereditary
X linked juvenile retinoschisis
Familial foveal retinoschisis Exudative
Secondary to optic disc pit X linked juvenile retinoschisis Secondary to optic disc pit This type of retinoschisis is very common with a prevalence of up to 7 percent in normal persons. Its cause is unknown. It can easily be confused with retinal detachment by the non-expert observer and in difficult cases even the expert may have difficulty differentiating the two. Such differentiation is important since retinal detachment almost always requires treatment while retinoschisis never itself requires treatment and leads to retinal detachment (and hence to visual loss) only occasionally. Unfortunately one still sees cases of uncomplicated retinoschisis treated by laser retinopexy or cryopexy in an attempt to stop its progression towards the macula. Such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. There is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. There is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. Degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. There is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. But as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. It is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] Hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an X-linked genetic defect. The genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) or congenital retinoschisis. Affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] It is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. Schisis is derived from the Greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. However, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. If the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. Although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]
Section: Introduction
Retinoschisis is an eye disease characterized by the abnormal splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers, usually in the outer plexiform layer. Retinoschisis can be divided into degenerative forms which are very common and almost exclusively involve the peripheral retina and hereditary forms which are rare and involve the central retina and sometimes the peripheral retina. The degenerative forms are asymptomatic  and involve the peripheral retina only and do not affect the visual acuity. Some rarer forms result in a loss of vision in the corresponding visual field.[1] Almost all cases are X-linked recessive and caused by a mutation in the retinoschisin gene (RS1).[2]

llm.short_answer: Retinoschisis is an abnormal splitting of the retinal layers; its genetic causes are mutations in the RS1 gene leading to defective retinoschisin and X-linked juvenile retinoschisis.
llm.long_answer: Reference: [GG_10], [CRAWL_WIKI_1], [CRAWL_WIKI_2]. Detailed explanation: Retinoschisis is an eye condition characterized by the splitting of the neurosensory layers of the retina, often occurring in the outer plexiform layer. The condition has both degenerative and hereditary forms. The hereditary form, known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS), is caused by a mutation in the RS1 gene, which results in a defective retinoschisin protein. This genetic defect is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner, primarily affecting young males.

Hereditary
X linked juvenile retinoschisis
Familial foveal retinoschisis Exudative
Secondary to optic disc pit X linked juvenile retinoschisis Secondary to optic disc pit This type of retinoschisis is very common with a prevalence of up to 7 percent in normal persons. Its cause is unknown. It can easily be confused with retinal detachment by the non-expert observer and in difficult cases even the expert may have difficulty differentiating the two. Such differentiation is important since retinal detachment almost always requires treatment while retinoschisis never itself requires treatment and leads to retinal detachment (and hence to visual loss) only occasionally. Unfortunately one still sees cases of uncomplicated retinoschisis treated by laser retinopexy or cryopexy in an attempt to stop its progression towards the macula. Such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. There is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. There is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. Degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. There is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. But as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. It is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] Hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an X-linked genetic defect. The genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) or congenital retinoschisis. Affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] It is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. Schisis is derived from the Greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. However, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. If the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. Although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]
Section: Introduction
Retinoschisis is an eye disease characterized by the abnormal splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers, usually in the outer plexiform layer. Retinoschisis can be divided into degenerative forms which are very common and almost exclusively involve the peripheral retina and hereditary forms which are rare and involve the central retina and sometimes the peripheral retina. The degenerative forms are asymptomatic  and involve the peripheral retina only and do not affect the visual acuity. Some rarer forms result in a loss of vision in the corresponding visual field.[1] Almost all cases are X-linked recessive and caused by a mutation in the retinoschisin gene (RS1).[2]

Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

llm.short_answer: An eye disease with abnormal splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers caused by an X-linked mutation in the RS1 gene
llm.long_answer: Reference: [CRAWL_WIKI_1], [CRAWL_WIKI_2]. Detailed explanation: Retinoschisis is an eye disease marked by a splitting of the retina’s neurosensory layers, often in the outer plexiform layer. It can occur in degenerative forms that affect the peripheral retina and hereditary forms that typically involve the central retina. The hereditary form of retinoschisis, usually seen in childhood, is primarily due to an X-linked genetic defect resulting in a mutation in the RS1 gene, which encodes the retinoschisin protein. This protein is crucial for maintaining the structural integrity of the retina.

Section: Classification
Hereditary
X linked juvenile retinoschisis
Familial foveal retinoschisis Exudative
Secondary to optic disc pit X linked juvenile retinoschisis Secondary to optic disc pit This type of retinoschisis is very common with a prevalence of up to 7 percent in normal persons. Its cause is unknown. It can easily be confused with retinal detachment by the non-expert observer and in difficult cases even the expert may have difficulty differentiating the two. Such differentiation is important since retinal detachment almost always requires treatment while retinoschisis never itself requires treatment and leads to retinal detachment (and hence to visual loss) only occasionally. Unfortunately one still sees cases of uncomplicated retinoschisis treated by laser retinopexy or cryopexy in an attempt to stop its progression towards the macula. Such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. There is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. There is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. Degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. There is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. But as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. It is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] Hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an X-linked genetic defect. The genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) or congenital retinoschisis. Affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] It is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. Schisis is derived from the Greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. However, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. If the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. Although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]
Section: Introduction
Retinoschisis is an eye disease characterized by the abnormal splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers, usually in the outer plexiform layer. Retinoschisis can be divided into degenerative forms which are very common and almost exclusively involve the peripheral retina and hereditary forms which are rare and involve the central retina and sometimes the peripheral retina. The degenerative forms are asymptomatic  and involve the peripheral retina only and do not affect the visual acuity. Some rarer forms result in a loss of vision in the corresponding visual field.[1] Almost all cases are X-linked recessive and caused by a mutation in the retinoschisin gene (RS1).[2]

Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

Section: Classification
Hereditary
X linked juvenile retinoschisis
Familial foveal retinoschisis Exudative
Secondary to optic disc pit X linked juvenile retinoschisis Secondary to optic disc pit This type of retinoschisis is very common with a prevalence of up to 7 percent in normal persons. Its cause is unknown. It can easily be confused with retinal detachment by the non-expert observer and in difficult cases even the expert may have difficulty differentiating the two. Such differentiation is important since retinal detachment almost always requires treatment while retinoschisis never itself requires treatment and leads to retinal detachment (and hence to visual loss) only occasionally. Unfortunately one still sees cases of uncomplicated retinoschisis treated by laser retinopexy or cryopexy in an attempt to stop its progression towards the macula. Such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. There is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. There is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. Degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. There is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. But as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. It is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] Hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an X-linked genetic defect. The genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) or congenital retinoschisis. Affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] It is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. Schisis is derived from the Greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. However, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. If the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. Although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]
Section: Introduction
Retinoschisis is an eye disease characterized by the abnormal splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers, usually in the outer plexiform layer. Retinoschisis can be divided into degenerative forms which are very common and almost exclusively involve the peripheral retina and hereditary forms which are rare and involve the central retina and sometimes the peripheral retina. The degenerative forms are asymptomatic  and involve the peripheral retina only and do not affect the visual acuity. Some rarer forms result in a loss of vision in the corresponding visual field.[1] Almost all cases are X-linked recessive and caused by a mutation in the retinoschisin gene (RS1).[2]

Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

Section: Classification
Hereditary
X linked juvenile retinoschisis
Familial foveal retinoschisis Exudative
Secondary to optic disc pit X linked juvenile retinoschisis Secondary to optic disc pit This type of retinoschisis is very common with a prevalence of up to 7 percent in normal persons. Its cause is unknown. It can easily be confused with retinal detachment by the non-expert observer and in difficult cases even the expert may have difficulty differentiating the two. Such differentiation is important since retinal detachment almost always requires treatment while retinoschisis never itself requires treatment and leads to retinal detachment (and hence to visual loss) only occasionally. Unfortunately one still sees cases of uncomplicated retinoschisis treated by laser retinopexy or cryopexy in an attempt to stop its progression towards the macula. Such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. There is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. There is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. Degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. There is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. But as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. It is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] Hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an X-linked genetic defect. The genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) or congenital retinoschisis. Affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] It is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. Schisis is derived from the Greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. However, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. If the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. Although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]
Section: Introduction
Retinoschisis is an eye disease characterized by the abnormal splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers, usually in the outer plexiform layer. Retinoschisis can be divided into degenerative forms which are very common and almost exclusively involve the peripheral retina and hereditary forms which are rare and involve the central retina and sometimes the peripheral retina. The degenerative forms are asymptomatic  and involve the peripheral retina only and do not affect the visual acuity. Some rarer forms result in a loss of vision in the corresponding visual field.[1] Almost all cases are X-linked recessive and caused by a mutation in the retinoschisin gene (RS1).[2]

Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

Such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. There is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. There is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. Degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. There is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. But as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. It is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] Hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an X-linked genetic defect. The genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) or congenital retinoschisis. Affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] It is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. Schisis is derived from the Greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. However, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. If the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. Although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]

Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

Section: Classification
Hereditary
X linked juvenile retinoschisis
Familial foveal retinoschisis Exudative
Secondary to optic disc pit X linked juvenile retinoschisis Secondary to optic disc pit This type of retinoschisis is very common with a prevalence of up to 7 percent in normal persons. Its cause is unknown. It can easily be confused with retinal detachment by the non-expert observer and in difficult cases even the expert may have difficulty differentiating the two. Such differentiation is important since retinal detachment almost always requires treatment while retinoschisis never itself requires treatment and leads to retinal detachment (and hence to visual loss) only occasionally. Unfortunately one still sees cases of uncomplicated retinoschisis treated by laser retinopexy or cryopexy in an attempt to stop its progression towards the macula. Such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. There is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. There is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. Degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. There is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. But as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. It is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] Hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an X-linked genetic defect. The genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) or congenital retinoschisis. Affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] It is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. Schisis is derived from the Greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. However, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. If the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. Although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]
Section: Introduction
Retinoschisis is an eye disease characterized by the abnormal splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers, usually in the outer plexiform layer. Retinoschisis can be divided into degenerative forms which are very common and almost exclusively involve the peripheral retina and hereditary forms which are rare and involve the central retina and sometimes the peripheral retina. The degenerative forms are asymptomatic  and involve the peripheral retina only and do not affect the visual acuity. Some rarer forms result in a loss of vision in the corresponding visual field.[1] Almost all cases are X-linked recessive and caused by a mutation in the retinoschisin gene (RS1).[2]

- Reference: [CRAWL_WIKI_2] - Information about: Retinoschisin - Wikipedia
Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

Section: Classification
Hereditary
X linked juvenile retinoschisis
Familial foveal retinoschisis Exudative
Secondary to optic disc pit X linked juvenile retinoschisis Secondary to optic disc pit This type of retinoschisis is very common with a prevalence of up to 7 percent in normal persons. Its cause is unknown. It can easily be confused with retinal detachment by the non-expert observer and in difficult cases even the expert may have difficulty differentiating the two. Such differentiation is important since retinal detachment almost always requires treatment while retinoschisis never itself requires treatment and leads to retinal detachment (and hence to visual loss) only occasionally. Unfortunately one still sees cases of uncomplicated retinoschisis treated by laser retinopexy or cryopexy in an attempt to stop its progression towards the macula. Such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. There is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. There is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. Degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. There is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. But as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. It is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] Hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an X-linked genetic defect. The genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) or congenital retinoschisis. Affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] It is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. Schisis is derived from the Greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. However, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. If the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. Although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]
Section: Introduction
Retinoschisis is an eye disease characterized by the abnormal splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers, usually in the outer plexiform layer. Retinoschisis can be divided into degenerative forms which are very common and almost exclusively involve the peripheral retina and hereditary forms which are rare and involve the central retina and sometimes the peripheral retina. The degenerative forms are asymptomatic  and involve the peripheral retina only and do not affect the visual acuity. Some rarer forms result in a loss of vision in the corresponding visual field.[1] Almost all cases are X-linked recessive and caused by a mutation in the retinoschisin gene (RS1).[2]

Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

Section: Classification
Hereditary
X linked juvenile retinoschisis
Familial foveal retinoschisis Exudative
Secondary to optic disc pit X linked juvenile retinoschisis Secondary to optic disc pit This type of retinoschisis is very common with a prevalence of up to 7 percent in normal persons. Its cause is unknown. It can easily be confused with retinal detachment by the non-expert observer and in difficult cases even the expert may have difficulty differentiating the two. Such differentiation is important since retinal detachment almost always requires treatment while retinoschisis never itself requires treatment and leads to retinal detachment (and hence to visual loss) only occasionally. Unfortunately one still sees cases of uncomplicated retinoschisis treated by laser retinopexy or cryopexy in an attempt to stop its progression towards the macula. Such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. There is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. There is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. Degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. There is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. But as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. It is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] Hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an X-linked genetic defect. The genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) or congenital retinoschisis. Affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] It is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. Schisis is derived from the Greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. However, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. If the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. Although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]
Section: Introduction
Retinoschisis is an eye disease characterized by the abnormal splitting of the retina's neurosensory layers, usually in the outer plexiform layer. Retinoschisis can be divided into degenerative forms which are very common and almost exclusively involve the peripheral retina and hereditary forms which are rare and involve the central retina and sometimes the peripheral retina. The degenerative forms are asymptomatic  and involve the peripheral retina only and do not affect the visual acuity. Some rarer forms result in a loss of vision in the corresponding visual field.[1] Almost all cases are X-linked recessive and caused by a mutation in the retinoschisin gene (RS1).[2]

- Reference: [CRAWL_WIKI_2] - Information about: Retinoschisin - Wikipedia
Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.

Familial foveal retinoschisis Exudative
Secondary to optic disc pit X linked juvenile retinoschisis Secondary to optic disc pit This type of retinoschisis is very common with a prevalence of up to 7 percent in normal persons. Its cause is unknown. It can easily be confused with retinal detachment by the non-expert observer and in difficult cases even the expert may have difficulty differentiating the two. Such differentiation is important since retinal detachment almost always requires treatment while retinoschisis never itself requires treatment and leads to retinal detachment (and hence to visual loss) only occasionally. Unfortunately one still sees cases of uncomplicated retinoschisis treated by laser retinopexy or cryopexy in an attempt to stop its progression towards the macula. Such treatments are not only ineffective but unnecessarily risk complications. There is no documented case in the literature of degenerative retinoschisis itself (as opposed to the occasional situation of retinal detachment complicating retinoschisis) in which the splitting of the retina has progressed through the fovea. There is no clinical utility in differentiating between typical and reticular retinoschisis. Degenerative retinoschisis is not known to be a genetically inherited condition. There is always vision loss in the region of the schisis as the sensory retina is separated from the ganglion layer. But as the loss is in the periphery, it goes unnoticed. It is the very rare schisis that encroaches on the macula where retinopexy is then properly used.[4] Hereditary retinoschisis is derived from a defective retinoschisin protein, which is due to an X-linked genetic defect. The genetic form of this disease usually starts during childhood and is called X-linked juvenile retinoschisis (XLRS) or congenital retinoschisis. Affected males are usually identified in grade school, but occasionally are identified as young infants.[citation needed] It is estimated that this much less common form of retinoschisis affects one in 5,000 to 25,000 individuals, primarily young males. Schisis is derived from the Greek word meaning splitting, describing the splitting of the retinal layers from each other. However, schisis is a word fragment, and the term retinoschisis should be used, as should the term iridoschisis when describing splitting of the iris. If the retinoschisis involves the macula, then the high-resolution central area of vision used to view detail is lost, and this is one form of macular disease. Although it might be described by some as a "degeneration", the term macular degeneration should be reserved for the specific disease "age-related macular degeneration".[citation needed]

Section: Introduction
Retinoschisin also known as X-linked juvenile retinoschisis protein is a lectin[5][6] that in humans is encoded by the RS1 gene.[7] It is a soluble, cell-surface protein that plays an important role in the maintenance of the retina where it is expressed and secreted by retinal bipolar cells and photoreceptors,[8][9] as well as in the pineal gland.[10] Retinoschisin (RS1) is encoded by the gene RS1 located on the X chromosome at p22.1.[7] Young males who have an RS1 mutation are susceptible to retinoschisis, an X-linked eye disease which causes macular degeneration and can lead to a loss of vision.[5][9]
Section: Function
Retinoschisin is an extracellular protein that plays a crucial role in the cellular organization of the retina: it binds the plasma membranes of various retinal cells tightly to maintain the structure of the retina.[5] In addition to enabling cell-to-cell adhesion, it has been shown that retinoschisin interacts with the sodium/potassium-ATPase (Na/K-ATPase) which resides in the plasma membrane.[10] RS1 also plays a role in the regulation on intracellular MAP kinase signalling.[11]
Section: Clinical significance
Pathogenic mutations of this gene are responsible for X-linked retinoschisis an early-onset macular degeneration in males that results in a splitting of the inner layers of the retina and severe loss in vision.[14] Female carriers of the RS1 mutation do not show symptoms of X-linked juvenile retinoschisis, except in rare cases where the non-functional protein is expressed due to anomalous X-chromosome inactivation. In young males who carry a gene mutation, the disease presents itself as retinal cavities, splitting of inner retinal layers (also known as foveal schisis),[8][5] and defective synapse activity.[5][12] Retinas that lack mature retinoshisin develop these characteristics in up to 1 in 5,000 males.[11] There are over 200 mutations of RS1 recorded in the Retina International Mutation Database Archived 2020-01-23 at the Wayback Machine, most of which are not pathogenic.
